caveats: **The eight read actions do not set a typed result status on a normal read.** On Windows `processors` and `memory` declare one only when their WMI query itself FAILED (`unavailable`, `permission_denied` or `constrained`, with the cause), so a failed query is not mistaken for a host with no CPU or DIMM rows; a query that returned nothing stays undeclared. Every such sample line reads `UNDECLARED / UNKNOWN /` regardless of whether the underlying probe succeeded, partially failed, or hit an unsupported leg (e.g. Linux `system` reads `unknown` in the sample, because the capture ran unprivileged, and gets the same `UNDECLARED` status as a clean Windows read). A consumer must inspect the row content (`unknown` fields, the `drivers` action's `__truncated__` marker), not the status, to tell success from degradation. **A connected-but-empty WMI query now emits an explicit `unknown` row instead of silently emitting nothing** — a deliberate divergence from the plugin's pre-#3404 behavior, made so a consumer can distinguish "the probe ran and found nothing" from an unrelated dispatch failure (the `#3404 sentinel-row decision` comment above `wmi_query` in `hardware_plugin.cpp`). Do not revert this to match the old silent-gap behavior.

**Two legs are partial: `drivers` on macOS, `memory` on Linux and macOS.** `drivers` is not implemented on macOS. No public per-driver/kext enumeration API exists; the descriptor declares it `YUZU_SUPPORT_UNSUPPORTED` (the macOS `drivers` row of `kActionDescriptors` in `hardware_plugin.cpp`) and the macOS sample shows the house `unknown` row rather than a capture. `memory` is aggregate-only on Linux and macOS. Linux needs `dmidecode` (typically root) for per-DIMM detail and falls back to `/proc/meminfo`'s total when unavailable or unprivileged; the Linux sample (captured unprivileged, euid 1000, on bare metal) shows the aggregate `total` row because `dmidecode` exits non-zero without root. macOS has no public per-DIMM API at all and always reports the aggregate. **Some planned actions can never have a source.** On macOS there is no public source for `chassis`, `baseboard` or `machine_id` (the hardware UUID from `system` already identifies the machine), yet the Linux and macOS legs of all four new actions are advertised `planned`. The per-OS leg PRs move such legs to a typed `unsupported` with a reason; until then a consumer must read `<os>:planned` as "not read", never as "this host has no value". The appended `cpu`/`dimm` columns (`socket_designation`, `stepping`, `manufacturer`, `part_number`, `serial`) ride on every `cpu`/`dimm` row so downstream schemas are final; Windows fills them, and on Linux and macOS they are still always `-` because no leg reads them yet. **`drivers_inventory` on Linux derives its signed state from one flag, and only toward "unsigned".** `/sys/module/<module>/taint` holds the module's taint letters; `E` (an unsigned module was loaded) maps to `unsigned`. A module without `E` reads `-`, never `signed`: the kernel may not enforce signatures at all, so the absence of the flag proves nothing. Signer, INF name, hardware id and date have no Linux source and are always `-`; provider and class are the fixed literals `kernel` and `module`, as in `drivers`. A built-in module has no `version` file and reads `-`. A module unloaded between the `/proc/modules` read and its `/sys/module` read also reads `-` (a normal race, not recorded as a failure); a refused or failed `/sys` read is recorded as a status token. Windows: Hitting the cap sets `windows:drivers_inventory:row_cap` and a `constrained` status (the rows read are still emitted). Many `Win32_PnPSignedDriver` rows carry only a hardware id (a device with no driver bound, for example `ACP HDA Node` on the capture host): every other field of those rows is `-`. `DriverDate` is accepted only as a CIM datetime or an ISO date; the locale-formatted text a PowerShell session prints (`21/06/2006 01:00:00`) cannot be read unambiguously and gives `-`. The row escaper folds a backslash to `/`, so a hardware id is written `ACPI/VEN_PNP&DEV_0C0C`. The Windows leg was exercised on a real Windows 11 host (an MSVC build, its unit tests and the capture in the Windows sample), with the personal identifiers in that capture redacted.

**Windows `disks.interface` reports the WMI-layer bus (`SCSI`), not the physical bus** — both drives in the Windows sample are NVMe/SATA but report `SCSI`, because `Win32_DiskDrive.InterfaceType` reports the storage stack layer WMI actually asks, not the physical connector. `disk_actions.smart` decodes the true bus (`nvme`/`sata`/`usb`) via a lower-level IOCTL and is the more accurate source when that distinction matters.

**`machine_id` is a keyed hash, not a secret.** The hash is HMAC-SHA256 under the fixed, public, versioned label `yuzu.machine-id.v1` (`agents/shared/machine_id_hash.hpp`, algorithm token `hmac-sha256-app-v1`), the application-specific derivation `machine-id(5)` recommends. It is NOT byte-compatible with systemd's `sd_id128_get_machine_app_specific` (which keys on the machine-id and returns 128 bits), so a Linux leg must call `hash_machine_id`, never libsystemd. It keeps the raw `MachineGuid` from leaving the host and stays stable across an agent reinstall or state wipe; it does NOT protect against a party that already holds the raw identifier, who can recompute it. It is also only as unique as the identifier: devices cloned from an image that was not generalised share a `MachineGuid` and so a hash, an OS re-image regenerates it, and the nil GUID (WinPE, a broken sysprep) is reported `unavailable` (`windows:machine_guid:nil`) rather than hashed. Do not use it as a primary key. The label and token are a cross-OS contract pinned by `tests/unit/test_hmac_sha256.cpp`.

**The Windows estate reads are honest, not complete.** `swap.total_mb` is the configured `MaximumSize` when the page file has one, which is stable. A system-managed page file has none, so the total is `AllocatedBaseSize`, which the OS grows under memory pressure; on such a host the daily value can change between cycles and cause a full upload. It cannot be made stable without inventing a number. Two further flaps can occur: a transient fault on the optional `Win32_PageFileSetting` query on a fixed-maximum host flips the total to the allocation and the section to `constrained` for that cycle, and a temporary page file (`Win32_PageFileUsage.TempPageFile`) can appear and disappear as an extra row; neither is filtered. `used_mb` is in the on-demand row only; the daily record never carries it. A chassis or baseboard serial, an asset tag, a socket label or a DIMM string that is empty or a known OEM filler (`smbios_parsers.hpp` `kPlaceholders`, matched whole and case-insensitively) is written `-` and the section stays `supported`; marking it `constrained` would present most OEM machines as incomplete. A filler string not in the table is reported verbatim, and a vendor serial of `00000000` is not recognised as filler. A string made only of bytes that are not valid UTF-8 (a `0xFF`-filled serial, even one padded with blanks) is treated as filler too, so it does not ship as a shared `????`; a literal `?`-only value is treated the same way. A text field longer than 256 bytes is cut on a character boundary before escaping. `GetSystemFirmwareTable('RSMB')` has no deadline parameter. It copies the SMBIOS table the kernel already holds from boot, with no device I/O, so it cannot wedge the way the synchronous volume ioctls can (#3925); the size is capped at 1 MiB and the probe/fill retry at three attempts (`agents/shared/win_rsmb.hpp`). If a measurement ever shows it blocking, the fix is `bounded_wait.hpp` in that one place. Windows derives `stepping` from the low nibble of CPUID EAX in `Win32_Processor.ProcessorId`; on arm64 it uses the class `Stepping` value when it is a plain decimal, else `-`.

definitions.description: Reports the baseboard (motherboard) vendor, product and serial number. Windows reads them from the SMBIOS Baseboard structure; a value the firmware leaves as OEM filler is reported as "-"; a text field is capped at 256 bytes. Linux and macOS do not read it yet: every dispatch answers one unsupported status row (linux:planned or macos:planned) until its leg lands, and macOS has no public source and will move to a typed unsupported. It is dispatched by the daily device-record sync: its status is recorded as the baseboard section, and the baseboard columns of the record fill from the row.
Returns BIOS or UEFI firmware details: vendor, version, and release date. Uses Win32_BIOS on Windows, /sys/class/dmi/id/bios_* on Linux, and system_profiler Boot ROM on macOS.

Reports the chassis type, serial number and asset tag. Windows reads them from the SMBIOS System Enclosure structure; a value the firmware leaves as OEM filler is reported as "-"; a text field is capped at 256 bytes. Linux and macOS do not read it yet: every dispatch answers one unsupported status row (linux:planned or macos:planned) until its leg lands, and macOS has no public source and will move to a typed unsupported. It is dispatched by the daily device-record sync: its status is recorded as the chassis section, and the chassis columns of the record fill from the row.

Lists physical disk drives with model name, capacity in GB, media type (SSD/HDD/Removable), and interface type (SCSI, NVMe, SATA, USB). Uses Win32_DiskDrive on Windows, native /sys/block on Linux, system_profiler on macOS.

Lists installed device drivers with name, version, date, provider, and device class. Uses Win32_PnPSignedDriver on Windows (the canonical signed-driver registry; the query can take several seconds) and a direct read of /proc/modules on Linux (module names only — version/date are not available without a per-module walk). Not supported on macOS (no public per-driver/kext enumeration API). Supports fleet queries like "devices running driver X older than version Y".

Lists installed drivers in a stable order (sorted by name, INF, hardware id, version; exact duplicates removed) with version, date, provider, device class, signer, signed state, INF name and hardware id. Always leads with one status row: supported when the read was complete, constrained with reason tokens when it was cut short (a row cap of 4096, a refused or failed read), unsupported on macOS. A value that could not be read is "-", never a guess. Windows reads Win32_PnPSignedDriver (bounded WMI, 4096 rows); a device with no driver bound shows only its hardware id. Linux reads /proc/modules plus /sys/module/<module>/version and taint with bounded no-follow reads: the signed state is "unsigned" only when the module's taint flags contain E, and "-" otherwise (no flag proves a module signed); signer, INF, hardware id and date have no Linux source. Not supported on macOS (no public kext/dext enumeration API). The existing "drivers" instruction is unchanged. This is an on-demand question; it is not part of the daily sync.

Reports an HMAC-SHA256 hash of the operating system machine identifier. The raw identifier never leaves the host. The hash is an HMAC-SHA256 under a fixed, public, versioned label, so it is stable across reinstalls of the agent and is not secret from a party that already holds the raw identifier. Windows reads the registry MachineGuid. Linux and macOS do not read it yet: every dispatch answers one unsupported status row (linux:planned or macos:planned) until its leg lands, and macOS has no source beyond the hardware UUID that device.hardware.system reports and will move to a typed unsupported. It is dispatched by the daily device-record sync: its status is recorded as the machine id section, and the hashed machine id column of the record fills from the row.
Returns the system manufacturer string (e.g. "Dell Inc.", "Apple Inc.", "Lenovo"). Uses Win32_ComputerSystem on Windows, /sys/class/dmi/id/sys_vendor on Linux, sysctlbyname(3) on macOS.

Lists installed memory DIMMs with slot locator, capacity in MB, memory type (DDR3/DDR4/DDR5), and speed in MHz. Uses Win32_PhysicalMemory on Windows, dmidecode on Linux (falls back to /proc/meminfo total), sysctlbyname(3) hw.memsize on macOS.
Returns the system model or product name (e.g. "OptiPlex 7090", "MacBookPro18,1"). Uses Win32_ComputerSystem on Windows, /sys/class/dmi/id/product_name on Linux, sysctlbyname(3) hw.model on macOS.

Lists installed CPUs with model name, physical core count, logical thread count, and clock speed in MHz. Uses Win32_Processor on Windows, /proc/cpuinfo on Linux, sysctlbyname(3) on macOS. Returns one row per physical CPU socket.

Reports swap devices and page files with total and used size in MB. Windows reads Win32_PageFileUsage; the total is the configured maximum when the page file has one (Win32_PageFileSetting), else the current allocation, which a system-managed page file grows under memory pressure. No page file is a definitive answer (a supported status row and no data rows). Linux and macOS do not read it yet: every dispatch answers one unsupported status row (linux:planned or macos:planned) until its leg lands. It is dispatched by the daily device-record sync: its status is recorded as the swap section, and its rows land in that section (used size is live telemetry and is not recorded).

Returns the machine's hardware serial number and system (SMBIOS / firmware) UUID — the stable CMDB correlation key (e.g. for ServiceNow reconciliation). Windows reads Win32_BIOS.SerialNumber and Win32_ComputerSystemProduct.UUID via WMI; Linux reads /sys/class/dmi/id/product_serial and product_uuid (0400, via the agent's cap_dac_read_search capability); macOS reads IOPlatformSerialNumber and IOPlatformUUID via native IOKit (IOServiceGetMatchingService + IORegistryEntryCreateCFProperty against IOPlatformExpertDevice). An absent value (e.g. a VM with no SMBIOS serial) returns the literal "unknown". This is the building block the device_ci daily-sync source (ADR-0016) collects in-process.

description: Reports hardware inventory: manufacturer, model, BIOS, CPU, memory, disks, drivers, chassis, baseboard, swap, machine id
how_it_works:
Thirteen independent actions, dispatched by action name (`HardwarePlugin::execute` and `dispatch` in `hardware_plugin.cpp`). `manufacturer`/`model`/`processors`/`system` are single native calls per OS (WMI, `sysctlbyname`/IOKit, or a `/sys`/`/proc` file read) with no subprocess. `bios` and `disks` need data no native API on macOS exposes, so those two legs shell out through the agent's bounded subprocess runner (`run_bounded_subprocess`, fixed deadline, no shell) to `system_profiler` and parse its output with a pure header-only parser (`hardware_macos_bios.hpp`, `hardware_disks_macos.hpp`). `memory` tries `dmidecode` on Linux (also via the bounded runner) and falls back to `/proc/meminfo`'s aggregate total when `dmidecode` is missing or fails. `drivers` enumerates `Win32_PnPSignedDriver` on Windows or reads `/proc/modules` on Linux; it is not implemented on macOS (no public per-driver/kext enumeration API). `drivers_inventory` is its stable-ordered, bounded sibling (the `drivers` action and its rows are unchanged): it adds signer, signed state, INF name and hardware id, sorts every row by (name, INF, hardware id, version), removes exact duplicates, and always leads with one `status|drivers_inventory|<supported|constrained|unsupported>|<tokens or ->` row followed by `driver_inv|<name>|<version>|<date>|<provider>|<class>|<signer>|<signed>|<inf>|<hwid>` rows, `-` standing in for any value that is absent. Windows runs one bounded WMI query on `Win32_PnPSignedDriver` (nine properties, `WHERE DeviceName IS NOT NULL`, a 4096-row cap rather than the 512-row cap the other actions use). Linux reads `/proc/modules` (bounded to 1 MiB, module names validated to `[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}`) and, under one opened `/sys/module` directory descriptor, `<module>/version` and `<module>/taint` with 256-byte no-follow reads; no subprocess runs and no `.ko` file is opened. Ordering, de-duplication, escaping and the status row are one pure header (`hardware_drivers_inventory.hpp`) shared by both legs. The four newest actions (`chassis`, `baseboard`, `swap`, `machine_id`) are read on Windows by `hardware_estate_win.cpp`: `chassis` and `baseboard` decode the SMBIOS table (`GetSystemFirmwareTable('RSMB')` through the shared reader `agents/shared/win_rsmb.hpp` and the shared walker `agents/shared/smbios_parsers.hpp`), `machine_id` reads the registry `MachineGuid` and ships only an HMAC of it, and `swap` reads `Win32_PageFileUsage` (plus `Win32_PageFileSetting` for the configured maximum) through the bounded WMI helper. Every decision about a row (placeholder handling, the stable swap total, the outcome) is in the pure `hardware_estate_parsers.hpp`, unit-tested on every host. On Linux and macOS they still answer exactly one `status|<action>|unsupported|<os>:planned` row from the shared planned-leg reporter (`agents/shared/planned_leg.hpp`, called from the dispatch in `hardware_plugin.cpp`) until those legs land. On Windows `processors` and `memory` also fill their appended columns (`socket_designation`, `stepping`; `manufacturer`, `part_number`, `serial`) from the WMI classes their rows already come from.

Every action that can find nothing still emits one row carrying the literal `unknown` in place of an unread value (the `manufacturer|unknown`, `model|unknown` and `bios_*|unknown` rows in `do_manufacturer`, `do_model` and `do_bios` and equivalents) — never a silent zero-row output — so a consumer can tell "the probe ran and found nothing" from "this action produced no output for an unrelated reason." This plugin is deliberately not a live-monitoring feed: every action is a point-in-time read with no polling, no event stream, and (except `drivers` and `drivers_inventory`, whose WMI query can take several seconds) no expectation of taking more than a few milliseconds.

columns.description: Swap device or page-file path, or "-" when absent. Backslashes are written as "/" (the plugin row escape), so C:\pagefile.sys reads C:/pagefile.sys. Status rows: the action name.
columns.name: device

columns.description: Total size in MB, or "-" when unread. Status rows: the level (supported, constrained or unsupported).
columns.name: total_mb

columns.description: Used size in MB, or "-" when unread. Status rows: the reason token (<os>:planned until the leg lands, a failure token on a degraded read, or "-").
columns.name: used_mb

columns.description: Where the value was read from, or "-" when absent. Absent on status rows.
columns.name: source

columns.description: Hardware serial number, or "unknown" when absent (e.g. a VM with no SMBIOS serial) or unreadable. Values: free text, or the sentinel "unknown".
columns.name: serial

columns.description: SMBIOS/firmware system UUID, or "unknown" when absent or unreadable. Values: free text UUID, or the sentinel "unknown".
columns.name: system_uuid

outputs_note: Pipe-delimited rows, one per record via `write_output()`. Scalar actions (`manufacturer`, `model`) emit `key|value`; the rest emit one or more `key|field1|field2|...` rows. A field the underlying probe could not read is the literal string `unknown` rather than an omitted field or an empty row — this applies to every read action's identity/value fields (`manufacturer`, `model`, `bios`, `processors`, `memory`, `disks`, `system`); `processors` rows end in two appended columns (`socket_designation`, `stepping`) and `memory` rows in three (`manufacturer`, `part_number`, `serial`); Windows fills them, and each is the literal `-` where the firmware or module reports filler or nothing, and on Linux and macOS until those legs read them. The four estate actions emit one typed status row first (`status|<action>|<supported|constrained|unsupported>|<token or ->`) and then their data rows; on Linux and macOS today the status row is `status|<action>|unsupported|<os>:planned` and nothing else. In an estate data row `-` means *absent* (the firmware reports no value or OEM filler such as `To Be Filled By O.E.M.`), which leaves the section `supported`; a field that could not be read is never written as a value. `drivers` additionally emits `__truncated__` in the name field when the Windows WMI row cap (512, `agents/shared/wmi_bounded.hpp`) is hit (the `__truncated__` comment in `do_drivers`, `hardware_plugin.cpp`).

privileges.grant: None documented for this plugin (the `hardware.*` row of `docs/agent-privilege-model.md`)
privileges.if_refused: The pre-existing actions: a WMI query that returns `error` falls back to its `unknown` sentinel row (the `wmi_query` helper in `hardware_plugin.cpp`), except that `processors` and `memory` also declare a typed status when their WMI query itself failed. The four estate actions instead report a typed `permission_denied` (no rows, no sentinel) for a refused SMBIOS, registry or WMI read

privileges.grant: `system` reads `/sys/class/dmi/id/product_serial` + `product_uuid` (mode `0400`); the packaged systemd unit grants the agent `CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH` as an ambient capability (bounding set limited to that one capability, `NoNewPrivileges` kept), and the dev install script sets `cap_dac_read_search+eip` on the binary instead (the capability comment in `do_system`, `hardware_plugin.cpp`). The agent clears its inheritable and ambient sets at start, so an exec'd child such as `dmidecode` does not inherit the capability (the in-process read is deliberate). Without the capability (opt-out, `--no-setcap`, or a manual launch) both fields read back `unknown`. The unit also keeps a root-made copy of the firmware tables under `/var/lib/yuzu-agent/dmi/`; this plugin does not read it. Not yet tested on systemd 239 (RHEL 8). `memory`'s `dmidecode` branch typically needs root and fails EPERM unprivileged, silently falling through to the `/proc/meminfo` total (the EPERM-fallback comment in `do_memory`, `hardware_plugin.cpp`).

result_status.when: The read completed. Firmware filler and an empty value are written `-` and do not lower the status; no page file at all is a definitive answer, not a failure.

The read failed or came back partial: a truncated or malformed table or structure (including a table whose walk stopped on a framing fault after the chassis or baseboard structure had decoded: that row is kept, but the section is never reported complete), an oversized table, a size race, a Win32 or WMI fault, or a failed `Win32_PageFileSetting` query (rows are kept, the total may then be the allocation).
A read was refused (`ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED`, WBEM access denied). No rows.
The source does not exist on this host (no RSMB provider, no `MachineGuid` value, a missing WMI class), or the leg has not landed (`<os>:planned`: one unsupported status row). No rows.

result_status.provenance: the read was cut short or partly refused; the rows that were read are still emitted
result_status.when: `linux:drivers_inventory:row_cap`, `windows:drivers_inventory:row_cap` (4096 rows reached), `linux:drivers_inventory:permission_denied` (EACCES/EPERM on `/proc/modules` or a `/sys/module` file), `linux:drivers_inventory:read_failed` (any other failed read, including a symlinked attribute), `linux:drivers_inventory:invalid_module_name` (a module name outside the kernel alphabet was skipped), `linux:drivers_inventory:proc_modules_oversized`, `windows:drivers_inventory:<wmi error token>` (the query failed; no rows)

where_the_data_goes: **Instruction result, plus a daily-sync consumer for eleven of the thirteen actions.** Rows travel over the agent's mTLS gRPC channel as the command response and land in the ResponseStore, queryable at `/api/responses/{id}`. The `device_ci` daily-sync source (ADR-0016) additionally invokes `manufacturer`, `model`, `system`, `bios`, `processors`, `memory`, `disks`, `chassis`, `baseboard`, `machine_id` and `swap` in-process via `LocalDispatcher` and folds their output into its canonical CI record (`agents/core/src/sync_source_device_ci.hpp`), which the server reconstructs field-for-field (`server/core/src/device_ci_ingestion.cpp`). The four newest actions (`chassis`, `baseboard`, `swap`, `machine_id`) are optional sections of that record: each contributes its own status, the planned one included, and a failure in one never stops the report. `drivers` and `drivers_inventory` are not part of the record (`drivers_inventory` is an on-demand question with no gather block). the `device.hardware.system` description in `content/definitions/hardware.yaml` documents this for the `system` action specifically.

**Not consumed by** Echo, DEX, or metrics. `manufacturer`/`model`/`bios`/`processors`/`memory`/`disks` gather on a 3600s TTL; `drivers` and `system` on an 86400s TTL (`content/definitions/hardware.yaml`); nothing polls continuously.

**Sensitivity.** `system` rows carry the hardware serial number and SMBIOS/firmware UUID — direct, stable device identifiers; on Windows `chassis`, `baseboard` and `memory` rows now also carry the chassis, board and per-DIMM serial numbers and the asset tag, and `machine_id` carries a stable hash of the OS machine identifier. These identify a device, not a person: by owner ruling (2026-10-30) serial numbers and asset tags are device identifiers, not personal data, and the `machine_id` hash is an HMAC under a fixed public label, so anyone who already holds the raw identifier can recompute it. That ruling covered serial numbers and asset tags, not the hash: the `machine_id` hash is a permanent pseudonym for the device that links to any other data set holding the same `MachineGuid` (which any local user can read and other software collects), so treat it as a stable device identifier in a privacy review; `manufacturer`/`model`/`bios`/`disks` name the specific hardware but not a person; `drivers` and `drivers_inventory` rows name installed driver software (`name`/`provider`, plus `signer`, INF name and hardware id on `drivers_inventory`) — a software inventory by another route. No row carries a username or account name.

**Siblings:** `device_identity` (domain/OU join state, same Wave 3 native-acquisition migration), `disk_actions` (SMART health and volume-to-drive mapping — `hardware.disks` reports the drive inventory, `disk_actions` reports its health and logical mounts).

**MCP / REST.** Discover: `discover_plugins` (summary) → `yuzu://plugin-docs` (this page as data) → `discover_instructions` / `get_definition("device.hardware.system")`. Run: `execute_instruction {definition_id, parameters}`. Read: `/api/responses/{id}`.
